4427: Acts of Pilate known to Epiphanius

4431: The Gospel of Nicodemus retells Jesus' trial before Pilate, as if from official records written by Nicodemus, and adds a famous second part: Jesus descends to the realm of the dead, breaks its gates and leads Adam and the righteous out. It took shape in the fourth to sixth centuries. It was never Scripture, but it shaped medieval drama, art and the idea of the "harrowing of hell".
4432:
The first part, the *Acts of Pilate*, presents a courtroom drama. Pilate's wife warns him; the Roman standards bow to Jesus by themselves; people Jesus healed come forward as witnesses; Pilate repeatedly declares him innocent. After the crucifixion, Joseph of Arimathea is imprisoned and miraculously freed, and witnesses report the resurrection and ascension to the Jewish council. Pilate is presented sympathetically - a trend that led to his veneration as a saint in the Ethiopian and Coptic churches.

The second part, the *Descent into Hell*, is told by two sons of Simeon who were raised from the dead (compare Matt 27:52-53). Satan and Hades argue as a great light breaks in; the King of Glory enters, binds Satan, takes Adam by the hand, and leads the patriarchs and prophets to paradise, where they meet the penitent thief. The earliest Christian appeals to "Acts of Pilate" (Justin around 155) probably assumed a Roman archive record existed rather than quoting this book; Christian Acts of Pilate are first clearly attested around 375, after the persecuting emperor Maximinus Daia had spread a forged pagan "Acts of Pilate" in 312.
4433: Charges against Jesus; Pilate's wife's dream; the standards bow (chs. 1-2)
4434: Witnesses for Jesus: the healed testify (chs. 3-8)
4435: Pilate washes his hands; crucifixion with the two thieves, Dysmas and Gestas (chs. 9-11)
4436: Joseph of Arimathea imprisoned and freed (chs. 12-15)
4437: Reports of the resurrection and ascension before the council (chs. 13-16)
4438: Descent into Hell: Satan and Hades; the King of Glory breaks the gates; Adam and the saints freed (chs. 17-27)
4439: It is late (fourth century and after), anonymous despite claiming Nicodemus, and was never proposed as Scripture. It belongs to the apologetic and devotional literature of the imperial church. Its sympathy for Pilate and its legendary witnesses go far beyond the Gospels. (Pilate and his wife Procla are commemorated as saints in the Ethiopian and Coptic churches, partly through this tradition, but the book itself is not canonical there.)
4440: Its Descent into Hell gave vivid form to an old belief, confessed in the Apostles' Creed ("he descended into hell"), and stands behind the Orthodox Easter icon of the Anastasis, where Christ pulls Adam and Eve from their tombs over broken gates. In the medieval West it inspired mystery plays on the "harrowing of hell", sermons and poetry such as Langland's *Piers Plowman*. It also gave names to the two thieves (Dysmas and Gestas) and to the soldier Longinus.
4441: Falsely presented as Nicodemus' record; written centuries later.
4442: Fourth century or later in its current form.
4443: Orthodox in its basic beliefs; legendary in its details.
4444: Spread very widely in East and West, but as devotional reading.
4446: Claims to be translated from Hebrew records - a historical, not prophetic, claim.
4447: Tells the emperor he can check Jesus' crucifixion and miracles in the "Acts" recorded under Pilate - probably an appeal to assumed Roman records, not this book.
4448: Reports that Maximinus Daia circulated forged pagan "Memoirs of Pilate" insulting Christ and made schoolchildren learn them.
4449: Mentions Acts of Pilate used by Quartodecimans to date Easter - the first clear reference to a Christian Acts of Pilate.
4450: Nicodemus, the Pharisee who came by night, becomes the supposed recorder.
4451: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury Jesus; the book expands Joseph's story.
4452: Pilate's wife's dream, developed into a scene in court.

4466: Earliest likely for the Acts of Paul
4469: The Acts of Paul and Thecla tells of a young woman in Iconium who hears Paul preach about chastity, breaks off her engagement, and follows him. She survives being burned and thrown to wild beasts, baptises herself, and becomes a teacher. It is part of a longer second-century Acts of Paul that, according to Tertullian, was written by a church elder in Asia who was removed from office for it.
4470:
In Iconium, Thecla sits at her window for three days listening to Paul preach that blessed are those who keep themselves pure. Her fiance and mother have Paul arrested and Thecla condemned to burn; a storm puts out the fire. In Antioch she resists a powerful man, is thrown to the beasts, and a lioness protects her; seeing a pool of seals, she throws herself in, baptising herself in the name of Jesus Christ. Freed, she dresses like a man, finds Paul, is commissioned by him to "go and teach the word of God", and spends her life teaching near Seleucia. The episode contains the only ancient physical description of Paul: short, bald, bow-legged, with eyebrows meeting and a slightly hooked nose, "full of grace".

The Thecla story is the best-preserved part of the longer *Acts of Paul*, which also contains 3 Corinthians, a story of Paul and a baptised lion at Ephesus, and Paul's martyrdom in Rome under Nero. A large Greek papyrus in Hamburg (around 300) and a Coptic papyrus preserve parts of the whole.
4471: Paul arrives in Iconium; the beatitudes of chastity (chs. 1-6)
4472: Thecla listens at the window and leaves her fiance (chs. 7-14)
4473: Paul scourged and expelled; Thecla saved from the fire (chs. 15-25)
4474: In Antioch: assault by Alexander, the beasts, the lioness, self-baptism (chs. 26-39)
4475: Thecla finds Paul, is sent to teach, and dies in Seleucia (chs. 40-43)
4476: Wider Acts of Paul: 3 Corinthians, the baptised lion, martyrdom in Rome
4477: This is a case where the church knew who forged a book and why. Tertullian (*On Baptism* 17) answered people who used Thecla's example to argue that women could teach and baptise. He says the writing falsely called Paul's was composed by a presbyter in Asia who admitted he did it "out of love for Paul" and was removed from his office. Eusebius lists the Acts of Paul among the "spurious" books (3.25.4). So pseudonymity was known and rejected, even when the writer's motives were sincere and much of the content was orthodox. Its extreme praise of celibacy also went beyond Paul's own letters.
4478: Thecla became one of the most popular saints of the early church, honoured as "equal to the apostles" and "protomartyr" among women in the Eastern churches; a major pilgrimage shrine grew at Seleucia, visited by the pilgrim Egeria in the 380s. The story gave early Christian women a model of courage and vocation, and it is central to modern debates about women's roles in early Christianity. Its description of Paul shaped his portrayal in art.
4479: Written about Paul, not by him; the author was a known presbyter in Asia.
4480: Second century, a century after Paul.
4481: Mostly orthodox; its demand for sexual renunciation and Thecla's self-baptism raised objections.
4482: The Thecla story spread everywhere; the full Acts of Paul less so.
4483: Read in private devotion and on Thecla's feast; Hippolytus and Origen quote the Acts of Paul without rejecting it.
4484: No claim to inspiration; the author's exposure ended any authority.
4485: Says a presbyter in Asia wrote the work under Paul's name out of love for Paul, confessed, and was removed from office; rejects Thecla's example as a licence for women to teach and baptise.
4486: Quotes a saying from the Acts of Paul without disapproval.
4487: Lists the Acts of Paul among the spurious books.
4488: Calls the "Travels of Paul and Thecla" apocryphal and repeats Tertullian's report.
4489: Paul preached in Iconium and was driven out, the setting of the story.
4490: Paul recalls his persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra.
4491: Paul commends singleness as a gift; the Acts turn this into a near-requirement.
4492: Contrast: the debated restriction on women teaching, against Thecla's commission to teach.
4493: Hermogenes, who deserted Paul, appears as a false companion in the story.
4494: Demas, who left Paul, is the other false companion.
4495: Onesiphorus, whose household Paul greets, welcomes Paul in Iconium.
4501: Acts of the Holy Apostle Thomas
4506: The Acts of Thomas tells how the apostle Judas Thomas, called Jesus' twin, was sold as a slave and sent to India, where he preached, worked miracles and persuaded couples to give up sex, until a king had him killed. It was written in Syria in the early third century. It contains the beautiful "Hymn of the Pearl" and stands behind the tradition of Thomas founding the church in India.
4507:
The apostles divide the world by lot and Thomas draws India, but refuses to go; Jesus sells him as a carpenter-slave to an Indian merchant. At a royal wedding Thomas persuades the bride and groom to live in chastity. He is commissioned to build a palace for King Gundaphorus, gives the money to the poor, and explains he has built the king a palace in heaven. Thirteen "acts" follow, with talking animals, demons and conversions, ending with Thomas speared to death on the orders of King Misdaeus because he converted the king's wife and family to celibacy. His bones are later taken to the West.

The book teaches that salvation means awakening the soul and renouncing marriage, wealth and the world (a strict ascetic outlook called encratism). Its "Hymn of the Pearl", sung by Thomas in prison, tells of a prince sent to Egypt to fetch a pearl, who forgets himself until a letter wakes him: a parable of the soul's exile and return, often read as Gnostic-leaning. The Manichaeans valued the work, which made later church leaders suspicious.
4508: Thomas sold as a slave to go to India (act 1)
4509: The wedding at Andrapolis and the bridal chamber vision (act 1)
4510: The heavenly palace for King Gundaphorus (act 2)
4511: Serpents, demons, a talking colt and the raising of the dead (acts 3-8)
4513: Conversions in the house of King Misdaeus; baptism and anointing rites (acts 9-13)
4515: It is a third-century romance with no apostolic author, and its insistence that married believers renounce sex conflicts with apostolic teaching on marriage. Its popularity among the Manichaeans and other dualist groups led writers such as Epiphanius and Augustine to treat apostolic Acts like this as heretical, and the Gelasian Decree rejected Acts under Thomas' name. In the Syriac churches, which honour Thomas highly, it was valued as story and its prayers influenced liturgy, but it was not Scripture.
4516: The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to Thomas, and the Acts are the earliest written form of the India mission tradition. Coins confirm a real Indo-Parthian king Gondophares in the first century AD, showing the author used genuine historical memory, though this does not prove the mission. Its baptism and anointing prayers are important evidence for early Syriac worship, and the Hymn of the Pearl is a literary treasure.
4517: A story about Thomas, not a writing claimed to be by him.
4519: Not openly heretical but strongly ascetic and docetic-leaning in places; prized by Manichaeans.
4520: Translated widely (Greek, Latin, Armenian, Ethiopic), but as legend.
4521: Mentions Acts of Andrew, John and other apostles among works used by heretics, "absurd and impious".
4522: Says encratite groups use Acts of Andrew, John and Thomas.
4523: Lists Acts under the name of the apostle Thomas among books not to be received.
4524: Thomas is called Didymus, "the twin"; the Acts make him Jesus' twin in appearance.
4525: The doubting Thomas of John becomes the missionary to the far East.
4526: The pearl of great price lies behind the Hymn of the Pearl.
4527: The prince who forgets himself in a far country and returns echoes the prodigal son.
4528: Contrast: Paul tells married couples not to deprive each other; the Acts urge married couples to renounce sex.
4529: Treasure in heaven: the palace built for the king in heaven.
4538: Asia Minor (possibly Ephesus or Smyrna) or Egypt
4539: The Acts of John tells of the apostle John's work in Ephesus: raising the dead, destroying the temple of Artemis by prayer, and even ordering bedbugs out of his bed. In its middle it includes a strange section where Jesus leads the disciples in a round dance and says he did not really suffer on the cross. Because of that teaching the church rejected it, and a council in 787 ordered it burned.
4540:
John travels to Ephesus and raises Cleopatra and her husband Lycomedes, who then commissions a portrait of John - which John scolds as a dead image of the body. In the temple of Artemis he prays and the altar shatters and part of the temple collapses. In a comic episode he tells the bedbugs in an inn to leave so he can sleep; in the morning they are waiting obediently at the door. The story of Drusiana, whom a young man tries to violate in her tomb, ends with repentance and resurrection. Finally John has a grave dug, lies down in it and peacefully dies.

The central section (chs. 87-105) is the reason for the book's fame and its rejection. John says Jesus looked different to different people, sometimes small, sometimes reaching to heaven, and that his body was sometimes solid and sometimes immaterial. Before his arrest Jesus leads a hymn while the disciples dance in a circle, answering "Amen". During the crucifixion Jesus appears to John in a cave on the Mount of Olives and shows him a "cross of light", saying that he did not suffer the things people will say of him. This is a clear form of docetism, the belief that Christ only appeared to have a human body.
4541: Arrival in Ephesus; raising of Cleopatra and Lycomedes (chs. 18-25)
4543: Healing old women; the fall of the temple of Artemis (chs. 30-45)
4546: John's teaching on Christ's changing appearance; the Hymn and round dance; the cross of light (chs. 87-105)
4547: John's last eucharist and peaceful death (chs. 106-115)
4548: Its docetic picture of Jesus - a Christ who did not truly suffer - contradicted the apostolic teaching that Jesus came in the flesh and died, and it had no apostolic author. Eusebius put "the Acts of Andrew and John" among heretical works (3.25.6). Later writers linked it to a Leucius, supposedly a companion of John. Most strikingly, the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, when iconoclasts quoted the portrait episode against icons, condemned the Acts of John and ordered that no one should copy it and that copies be burned - which partly explains why the text survives only in fragments.
4549: Historians value it as evidence of second-century docetic Christianity and of early Christian hymns and dance. The Hymn of Jesus inspired Gustav Holst's choral work *The Hymn of Jesus* (1917). Its gentler stories - the bedbugs, the portrait, John's peaceful death - fed later legends about the beloved disciple in Ephesus.
4550: Not by John; later attributed to a "Leucius".
4552: Openly docetic in its central section.
4553: Known in several regions, mostly among dualist and ascetic groups.
4554: Not read in the church's worship; condemned.
4555: Claims to report secret revelation given to John.
4556: Names the Acts of Andrew and John among books of heretics, wholly out of keeping with apostolic style and teaching.
4557: Quotes part of the hymn as used by the Priscillianists and criticises it.
4559: Has the portrait passage read out, condemns the book, forbids copying it and orders copies burned.
4560: John as the disciple Jesus loved, reclining next to him.
4561: Contrast: the Gospel places the beloved disciple at the cross; the Acts place John in a cave, told that Jesus did not truly suffer.
4562: Contrast: 1 John makes confessing Jesus come in the flesh the test of truth - the very point the Acts deny.
4563: Contrast: "which our hands have handled" against the Acts' changeable, sometimes immaterial body.
4564: After singing a hymn they went out - the cue for the Acts' round-dance hymn.
4565: The conflict with Artemis' worship at Ephesus, here dramatised with the temple's collapse.
4576: The Acts of Peter tells of Peter's contest with the magician Simon Magus in Rome and his death. It gives us two famous scenes: Peter, fleeing Rome, meets Jesus and asks "Lord, where are you going?" (Quo vadis?), and Peter is crucified upside down at his own request. It is a late second-century story, not Scripture, but these scenes passed into Christian tradition and art.
4577:
After Paul leaves Rome for Spain, Simon Magus (the magician of Acts 8) arrives and wins over most of the church. God sends Peter, who defeats Simon in a series of contests: a dog speaks with a human voice, a smoked fish swims again, and the dead are raised. Finally Simon flies over the Forum; Peter prays and he falls and breaks his leg in three places, dying later. Peter's preaching of chastity persuades the concubines of the prefect Agrippa and other wives to leave their partners, which brings persecution. Peter flees Rome, meets the Lord entering the city and asks where he is going; Jesus answers that he is going to Rome to be crucified again. Peter returns, asks to be crucified head downward, and preaches a final sermon from the cross about the mystery of the cross.

Most of the text survives in a single Latin manuscript at Vercelli in Italy (sixth or seventh century); the martyrdom also survives in Greek and other languages. A Coptic story about Peter's paralysed daughter may also come from it.
4578: Paul leaves for Spain; Simon Magus leads the Roman church astray (chs. 1-4)
4580: Contests with Simon: the talking dog, the swimming fish, raising the dead (chs. 7-29)
4583: Peter crucified upside down; his speech on the cross (chs. 36-41)
4584: It was written over a century after Peter, by an unknown author, as an entertaining and edifying romance. Eusebius says no orthodox writer had used the "Acts" called Peter's (3.3.2) and puts them with the heretical books (3.25.6). Its teaching on the cross has some docetic and mystical elements and its demand for celibacy was extreme, so it was later linked with other rejected apostolic Acts and with Manichaean use.
4585: The Quo vadis story and the upside-down crucifixion became central to how Christians remember Peter. Origen, as reported by Eusebius (3.1.2), also says Peter asked to be crucified head down, and the chapel of Domine Quo Vadis on the Appian Way marks the legendary meeting. Caravaggio's *Crucifixion of Saint Peter* and many other works draw on it. Historians use it as evidence of second-century Roman Christian memory and of conflict stories about Simon Magus.
4586: A story about Peter by an unknown later writer.
4588: Mostly orthodox in tone, with some mystical, docetic-leaning teaching on the cross.
4590: Says the "Acts" bearing Peter's name were not handed down as recognised and no orthodox writer used them.
4592: Reports Origen's statement that Peter, at the end, was crucified head downward at his own request.
4593: Rejects Acts under the name of the apostle Peter.
4594: Simon the sorcerer of Samaria, whom Peter rebuked, becomes Peter's great opponent in Rome.
4595: Jesus foretells that Peter will stretch out his hands and be led where he does not want to go - read as predicting crucifixion.
4596: "Lord, whither goest thou?" - the Quo vadis question first asked at the Last Supper.
4597: Peter knows his death is near, as the Lord showed him.
4598: "Babylon" is widely read as Rome, linking Peter to the city.
4599: Paul's planned journey to Spain, which the Acts treat as having happened.
4612: The Apocalypse of Peter is a second-century vision in which Jesus shows Peter the punishments of sinners in hell and the joys of the righteous. It is the earliest Christian "tour of hell". For a time some churches read it alongside Revelation, and the Muratorian fragment mentions it, but it was eventually left out of the canon.
4613:
On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask Jesus about the signs of his coming. He warns of false messiahs, explains the parable of the fig tree, and then shows Peter the day of judgement: the dead rise, fire covers the earth, and each sinner receives a punishment that fits the sin - blasphemers hang by their tongues, murderers are tormented by worms, those who lent money at interest stand in pus and blood, and women who aborted or abandoned children face their children's accusations. Then the elect see paradise, and the work ends with a version of the transfiguration and ascension. The Ethiopic text also includes the startling idea that the righteous may ask for some of the damned to be saved - a passage that some read as an early hint of mercy beyond judgement.

The book was popular in the second and third centuries. Clement of Alexandria quotes it as Scripture. It survives as a Greek fragment found at Akhmim in 1886-87 (with the Gospel of Peter), in small Greek papyri, and in a fuller Ethiopic version within a larger work, discovered in 1910.
4614: On the Mount of Olives: signs of the end, false messiahs, the fig tree (chs. 1-2)
4615: The day of judgement: resurrection and cosmic fire (chs. 3-6)
4616: The places of punishment and the sins they fit (chs. 7-12)
4617: Mercy for some of the damned at the request of the righteous (ch. 14, Ethiopic; debated)
4618: The vision of paradise and the transfiguration (chs. 15-17)
4619: It never achieved wide enough acceptance and its claim to Peter's authorship was doubted. The Muratorian fragment says "we receive" the apocalypses of John and Peter, but adds that some will not allow the latter to be read in church. Eusebius placed it among the "spurious" books (3.25.4), and later lists drop it. Its vivid, mechanical punishments and its mercy passage also sat uneasily with developing doctrine. In the Ethiopian tradition the text survives inside a larger pseudo-Clementine work, so it was read, but it is not among the books of the Ethiopian canon; that status here is debated.
4620: It shaped Christian imagination about the afterlife for over a thousand years. Through the later *Apocalypse of Paul*, which borrowed from it, its tours of hell fed into medieval visions and ultimately Dante's *Inferno*. Sozomen in the fifth century reports that some churches in Palestine still read it once a year on Good Friday. It is also key evidence for early Christian views on abortion and on the question of universal mercy.
4622: Early second century, earlier than some other books that were debated.
4623: Orthodox in outline; its mercy passage and vivid punishments troubled later readers.
4624: Known in Rome, Alexandria and Palestine, but disputed.
